name: Nasal irrigation

lead: Nasal irrigation flushes the nasal passages with salt water to clear mucus and congestion. People interested in nasal breathing use it to keep the nose open, which some link to better sleep and to breathing habits that affect the face.

Saline passes in one nostril and out the other, moistening the lining and rinsing out mucus, allergens and debris. It is an established practice from Ayurvedic tradition and appears in guidelines as an adjunct for sinus and allergy symptoms. No study has looked at whether it changes how the nose looks.

paras: People use a neti pot, squeeze bottle or similar device with a saline solution, often as part of a daily or as-needed hygiene routine, especially during colds, allergy season or when the nose feels blocked. Relief from congestion is typically noticed within the same session.

Reviews describe irritation, stinging and nosebleeds as the usual side effects. Rare fatal infections, including amoeba infections, have followed use of untreated tap water, and health agencies advise sterile, distilled or boiled and cooled water and regular cleaning of the device.

web.title: FDA consumer update on neti pots

angle.text: A saline rinse clears mucus and congestion so the nose breathes more easily, which people link to better sleep and face habits. It is an established hygiene and medical practice. No studies have looked at its effect on nose appearance.

lead: Nasal irrigation, also called nasal lavage, sinus rinsing or neti pot use, is a hygiene and medical practice that flushes the nasal cavity with saline solution to clear mucus, allergens and debris.[1][2] It originated in Ayurvedic practice in India, where jala neti is traditionally part of daily personal hygiene (soucha).[1][2] Devices range from the ceramic neti pot to squeeze bottles, bulb syringes for children and electric irrigators.[1]

For appearance and breathing, the connection is a chain: a rinse thins and clears mucus, a clearer airway makes nasal breathing easier, and easier nasal breathing supports sleep and the facial look people associate with a rested, unblocked nose. Medical evidence centres on symptom relief. A 2015 guideline cited by Wikipedia supports irrigation for symptoms of acute sinusitis, a 2016 Cochrane review is reported to find weak evidence for chronic sinusitis, and a 2012 meta-analysis suggests temporary relief in allergic rhinitis.[1][3] Grokipedia describes guidelines and systematic reviews as supportive for chronic rhinosinusitis and allergic rhinitis.[2]

Nasal irrigation is discussed in communities concerned with nasal breathing, sleep and appearance as a way to keep the airway clear. No study cited here tests irrigation as an appearance intervention. The practice has a safety literature of its own: rare fatal infections have followed use of untreated tap water, and health agencies publish water-preparation guidance.[1]
infobox: Neti pot, squeeze bottle, bulb syringe, powered irrigator [1]
Use sterile, distilled or boiled and cooled water [1]

paras: The earliest record of nasal rinsing is in Indian Ayurveda, whose roots are traced to the Vedas. Jala neti, a yogic practice performed daily as part of personal hygiene, uses water poured through one nostril, while a related technique, sutra neti, uses a string.[1]

A study of US media coverage in Health Communication traces the neti pot's rise and its "Americanization" as a form of integrative medicine in news discourse, a period in which the device moved from yoga and Ayurveda circles to pharmacy shelves and television segments.[4] The same study frames later coverage of infection cases as a rupture in that story.[4]

Common devices are neti pots, squeeze bottles, bulb syringes (often for children) and electric irrigators. Saline is poured or pumped through one nostril and drains from the other [1]. Isotonic (0.9 percent) or hypertonic saline is used, and high-volume, low-pressure delivery is described as typical [2].

Laboratory studies compared how neti pots, squeeze bottles and pressurised sprays distribute solution in cadaver sinuses after endoscopic sinus surgery [5]. Computational and 3D-printed model studies simulate how irrigation fluid fills and coats the nasal airway [6][7][8].

Wikipedia describes a home saline recipe of about a quarter litre of tepid sterilised water with roughly half a level teaspoon of table salt, and notes that a steroid such as budesonide may be added to irrigation fluids for chronic rhinosinusitis under medical direction.[1] A randomised crossover study in 33 volunteers evaluated the safety and tolerability of a reformulated surfactant additive compared with buffered saline.[9]

Wikipedia reports that irrigation is generally well tolerated, with possible irritation, nosebleeds, headache and post-rinse drainage [1]. The main concern is infection from non-sterile water or unwashed devices. Fatal cases of amoebic infection linked to tap-water neti pot use were reported in 2011 and 2013, and a 2018 case involved Balamuthia infection after tap water filtered through a household purifier [1]. A case report describes pneumococcal meningitis associated with over-the-counter sinus irrigation [10].

Wikipedia summarises CDC guidance as four ways to make water safe: boiling for one minute and cooling (three minutes above 6,500 feet), filtering with a device labelled NSF 53 or NSF 58 or with an absolute pore size of one micron or smaller, buying distilled or sterile water, or disinfecting with chlorine bleach at the right level and contact time to kill Naegleria.[1] Grokipedia lists similar measures and advises cleaning devices after each use.[2] Research has also examined how much irrigation fluid remains in the nose and how medicines added to irrigation are absorbed.[11]

Tap water is not recommended because it can contain microbes that are harmless to swallow but dangerous in the nose.[1] The Cochrane review of allergic rhinitis describes irrigation as generally well tolerated.[12]

The US Food and Drug Administration describes neti pots and similar devices, including bulb syringes, squeeze bottles and battery-operated pulsed-water devices, as generally safe and effective when used and cleaned properly, for congestion from colds, allergies and sinus problems and for moistening nasal passages dried by indoor air [13].

FDA guidance advises rinsing only with distilled, sterile or previously boiled water. Acceptable options it lists are store-bought water labelled distilled or sterile, tap water boiled for three to five minutes then cooled and stored in a clean closed container for up to 24 hours, or water passed through a filter designed to capture harmful microbes [13]. It says tap water can contain bacteria and amoebas that are harmless to swallow but can survive in the nose and cause serious infections, which the CDC notes are rarely fatal [13].

The agency adds that plain water can irritate the nose while saline reduces burning, that people with weakened immune systems are advised to consult a health care provider first, and that devices should be washed and dried after use [13]. It distinguishes nasal spray bottles, which moisturise dry passages, from irrigation devices, which flush mucus, allergens and bacteria [13]. Problems with irrigation devices can be reported to the FDA MedWatch programme [13].

Evidence in encyclopedic summaries relates to sinus and allergy symptoms: a 2015 guideline update from the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation, a 2016 Cochrane review on chronic sinusitis and a 2012 meta-analysis in allergic rhinitis.[1][3] The Cochrane Database also published a 2018 systematic review of saline irrigation for allergic rhinitis, which searched for randomised trials comparing irrigation by any route, volume or tonicity with no treatment or other therapies.[12]

In children, a systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised trials with 569 participants found a benefit of saline irrigation for some nasal symptoms (standardised mean difference -0.29) but no significant improvement in respiratory symptoms.[14] A 2025 single-blind randomised trial enrolled children aged 6 to 12 with allergic rhinitis to evaluate normal saline irrigation.[15]

A pilot open-label randomised trial examined hypertonic saline irrigation and gargling for the common cold, and a 2025 randomised trial compared isotonic and hypertonic solutions after endoscopic sinus surgery in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis; a review covers irrigation after sinus surgery.[16][17][18]

Cadaver, computational and 3D-printed model studies address how fluid is distributed through the sinuses rather than patient outcomes.[5][6][7][8] No studies found on nasal irrigation as a way of changing the visible appearance of the nose.

Nasal irrigation sits in the sleep and breathing category of this wiki because congestion is discussed as something that interferes with nasal breathing and sleep. Wikipedia and the cited research do not document appearance-focused use, and no published research links irrigation to a change in nasal appearance.[1]

Fatal infections reported in connection with neti pots include two deaths from Naegleria fowleri in 2011, a Louisiana death from the same amoeba in 2013, and a 2018 Balamuthia mandrillaris infection after a month of irrigating with tap water filtered through a household purifier.[1] A 2020 case report describes pneumococcal meningitis associated with over-the-counter sinus irrigation.[10] Reported common effects are nasal irritation, nosebleeds, headache and post-rinse drainage.[1]
